Hi everyone,

We have just about wrapped up our project implementing an executable DenseMatrix type in Lean 4 along with a Gaussian elimination algorithm. Before opening pull requests, we would love to get feedback from the community on our approach and code structure.

Our main focus is computational performance on flat, contiguous memory structures, complementing Mathlib’s Matrix type. To avoid duplicating theory, we use a proof-by-transfer approach, defining a bijection between Matrix and DenseMatrix elements of the same dimension, and in particular, a ring isomorphism between the two types when they are representing square matrices. This way, algebraic properties can be transferred directly to and from Mathlib’s Matrix theory.

Proposed PR Breakdown:

Matrix Theory: Theory about echelon form and row equivalence, written for Mathlib Matrix. This includes uniqueness of the RREF and equivalence of notions of row equivalence and two matrices having the same null space. These live in the ProvableComputation.LinearAlgebra.Matrix folder.

DenseMatrix Data Type & Operations: Core contiguous data structure, typeclass instances, and optimized operations (addition, multiplication, etc.). These live in the ProvableComputation.LinearAlgebra.DenseMatrix.Basic file.

Gaussian Elimination: Verifiable row echelon form transformations and Gaussian elimination proofs. These live in the ProvableComputation.LinearAlgebra.DenseMatrix.GaussianElimination folder.

We are aware of recent discussion and PRs around computational linear algebra and would love to know how our work might align with or complement ongoing efforts.

You can find our repository here: https://github.com/josephqian507/DenseMatrix

Any feedback on design, code style, or PR sequencing would be greatly appreciated!
I think there is already a sequence of computation-focused Matrix being PRed. Like #43673. Though it looks like it is tactic-only and not meant for external usage
There is also some recent theory about echelon form https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Matrix/Echelon/Basic.html

@Weiyi Wang It looks like they do a good job building on the existing Mathlib definition docs#IsRowEchelon docs#IsReducedRowEchelon. See their Matrix.Echelon file.

I think that some of the basic lemmas about row equivalence like RowEquivalent.mul_eq_zero_iff, rowEquivalent_of_mul_eq_zero, rowEquivalent_iff_ker_eq are certainly appropriate for Mathlib PRs, although I would encourage the authors to try to golf these proofs and see if there are any reusable sublemmas that can be used to simplify them (especially reducing the usage of have). It would be great work towards the main result about the uniqueness of the reduced echelon form:

private theorem reduced_unique_of_rowEquivalent {m n : Nat} {B C : Matrix (Fin m) (Fin n) R}
(hBC : RowEquivalent B C) (hB : IsReducedRowEchelon B) (hC : IsReducedRowEchelon C) :
    B = C

As for the content about dense matrix theory, this is much harder to say since it would require adding new definitions and we need to think deeply about what it even means to be a dense matrix. For example, I'm not sure if this is the definition we would want in Mathlib:

/-- Flattened array representation of matrix. -/
structure DenseMatrix (m n : Nat) (α : Type u) where
  data : Vector α (m * n)
deriving Repr
Hi, just for curiosity, what are the performances of your design for example for verification of matrix products within the kernel?

Thank you for your feedback. We will improve the lemmas and begin the PR process for the matrix theory then.

@Weiyi Wang @Jack McCarthy regarding the DenseMatrix: the purpose of this data type is to efficiently run computations on matrix literals, hence the flattened array design. While I am not sure whether or not mathlib is the right place for such a definition, I do believe that it is a valuable addition to the Lean language as it expands on its computational capabilities. Our DenseMatrix seems to address a different problem than ListMatrix.

@Nicola Falciola we have not formally benchmarked verification, but I will work on that. Since the verification process functions by establishing an equivalence between DenseMatrix and the mathlib Matrix, the only thing that needs to be benchmarked is the equivalence (specifically, the semiring instance and ring isomorphism (line 697 and 755) for square matrices, and mul_toMatrix (line 685) for the general case.

As @Luigi Massacci pointed out, I'm also working on a dense linear algebra library NumLean supporting arbitrary rank tensors with CUTLASS/CuTe style interface.

NumLean is designed to do fast linear algebra on arrays of floating point numbers but also prove correctness over real numbers.

The core type is Tensor

structure Tensor (X : Type u) (I : Type v)
    {Ks K nX nI} [VectorType Ks K] [HasFlatRepr X Ks nX] [IndexType I nI] where
  data : Ks (nI * nX)

The usual values for those types are:

  • X is the element type, usually Float or Real but can also be for example Tensor Float Fin 10 for tensor of tensors
  • I is the index type,Fin n₁ × ... × Fin nᵣ for rank r tensor or Fin m × Fin n × ColorChannel for an image (where inductive ColorColorChannel where | red | green | blue)
  • K is base storage scalar, usually Float or Real
  • Ks is the flat array implementation, FloatVector (sized wrapper around FloatArray) or Vector Real

The main idea is to write program polymorphic in K and Ks, prove properties for K = Real and Ks = Vector Realand execute for K = Float and Ks = FloatVector.

This way you can write provably correct programs except rounding errors.

My goal is to provide equivalent of NumPy in the Lean ecosystem and provide some form of guaranteeing correctness but performance is more important. Right now, I do not know how to also give guarantees down to rounding errors without utterly sacrificing performance.

I'm happy to coordinate but I'm not exactly sure what is your goal for your DenseMatrix. With your definition

structure DenseMatrix (m n : Nat) (α : Type u) where
  data : Vector α (m * n)

you do have O(1) index access but calling it "contiguous data structure" is not entirely accurate as elements in Vector are boxed. Iterating over all element does not go over a contiguous block or memory which is crucial for numerical algorithms which are often memory bound. So probably your goals are different from my goals with NumLean.

Tomas Skrivan said:

Right now, I do not know how also give guarantees down to rounding errors without utterly sacrificing performance.

How dies this compare with TorchLean, which sounds similar in scope to NumLean? I think TorchLean ran into a similar issue, see section 2.3 where the discuss flexible floating points semantics with users choosing between R\mathbb{R}R vs. a Round-on-Rmodel vs interval arithmetic. @Robert Joseph then introduced FloatLib, which claims efficient execution but I expect it will still be slow for full proofs since there is a combinatorial explosion problem if you want to properly handle all of the rounding cases.

@Jack McCarthy I would say that the biggest difference is that NumLean uses Lean's runtime but TorchLean uses pytorch runtime(@Robert Joseph please correct me if I say anything wrong :) I'm not sure if I understand TorchLean well).

This has consequences on what you need to trust:

  • In TorchLean you write Lean/mathlib spec for PyTorch's functions and need to trust that the real number spec sufficiently well models PyTorch behavior in floats. You also need to check that the translation of the spec to PyTorch code is done correctly.
  • NumLean provides generic interfaces/classes in which the program is written. They can be instantiated with Float for execution and Real for proofs. Right now, you need to manually check that all the Float instances roughly match the Real instances. You also need to trust Lean native compiler.

Apart of trust/verification concerns, my motivation for NumLean is that you still have the full expressibility of Lean at your disposal and you are not boxed in PyTorch way of writing programs.

Oh and regarding the rounding errors. Yes there is a bunch of libraries doing interval arithmetic or formalizing floating point numbers. These are nice when working with few numbers but I don't see it scaling to vectors of millions of elements. I'm not expert on rounding errors, heck I don't even know what the "right" correctness statement is for a program computing sum of number ∑ i, x i.

Thanks @Tomas Skrivan and @Jack McCarthy! There’s quite a bit of overlap with what you describe for NumLean, and I wanted to clarify a few things about TorchLean :)

TorchLean’s CPU computations run in Lean. Lean also owns the model composition, differentiation tape and backward traversal. On CUDA, LibTorch supplies numerical primitives and local gradient operations, with LibTorch autograd disabled. Attention, for example, is composed in Lean from matrix products, masking and softmax, including its backward computation. We also support custom tensor functions written in Lean, with checked CUDA lowering for a supported subset. Several of these capabilities come from our recent updates, and I’ll be discussing the new features in more detail soon!

TorchLean is also polymorphic over the scalar type itself. Our tensors have the form Tensor α shape, and operations and model definitions are parameterized by α, with instances supplying the operations they need. This lets us reuse definitions across native floats, FloatLib’s configurable floating-point formats, exact rational algebraic computations, real-valued specifications, intervals and complex-valued computations. The complex type is itself parameterized: TorchLean.Complex α stores real and imaginary components of type α, so their representation and precision are configurable too. Through FloatLib, we can choose arbitrary valid binary precisions by configuring the exponent and fraction widths. There’s already a binary128 training example that keeps parameters, activations, gradients and SGD updates in that precision.

We follow PyTorch’s API and operator conventions where relevant, but many mathematical specifications come from the literature: the Transformer specification follows Vaswani et al., and the normalization specifications reference the original papers. These definitions are parameterized by the scalar context, allowing real-valued reasoning and floating-point execution, with the mathematical laws needed for proofs supplied separately. On rounding, FloatLib has proofs connecting executable arithmetic to its floating-point specifications, alongside bounds relative to real arithmetic. For large sums, those error bounds compose over reduction trees under the local rounding and range assumptions. The general proof doesn’t enumerate every possible rounding history, so that particular concern doesn’t apply to how these bounds are established. TorchLean reuses this theory, although the external numerical backend remains a trust boundary.

I also ran some local experiments with full arrays. On one Xeon CPU core, an FP32 sum took approximately 40 ms for one million elements and 3.99 s for 100 million. Dot products took 61.5 ms and 6.16 s, respectively. The corresponding C results matched bit-for-bit, although C was substantially faster: approximately 1.1 ms and 114 ms for the sums, and 1.12 ms and 122 ms for the dots. The dot products used separate multiplication and addition in both implementations. Million-element outward-rounded interval sums also completed, and I independently checked that both the FP32 and FP64 enclosures contained the exact rational sums.

Concrete proof evaluation is a separate measurement. We checked a sum of one million FP32 ones against its expected result: native_decide passed in 11.8 seconds. Direct kernel evaluation of the same computation was still running when we stopped it after 68 minutes, so we don’t yet know its completion time. Both proof checks used one CPU core; these were addition checks, separate from the dot-product execution benchmarks above. Native evaluation adds compiler trust, so these are different checking routes. In these small experiments, native evaluation was much faster. Making direct kernel evaluation fast is a difficult problem, and the representation of the computation matters too; we’re still investigating where we can improve it. Your point about boxed arrays and memory layout is relevant as well and we have thought about this a lot and exactly why we redesigned a lot of the torchlean core arrays to be more efficient, since those costs matter alongside the arithmetic itself. I’d be happy to compare concrete examples and discuss which pieces we could share between the projects :)
Thanks for the summary and corrections! I need to learn about TorchLean more. Anyway we should probably discuss this somewhere else :)

I thought it might be helpful to provide some additional contexts for the computational methods project. We are currently mainly focusing on efficient computation within the kernel itself, which helps to make more proofs that need these facts to be possible and checked efficiently (without native_decide etc). This sometimes requires different designs from methods that optimise for the speed of the compiled code, such as the choice of 2D-List representation in #43673 for easier induction and formulating the algorithms that the kernel needs to run, without needing random access to elements. I chose to leave this family of definitions and operations under Tactic/ as they should be considered as metaprogramming helpers, which also prevents accidental misuses in the main theory, since the above cost might not be obvious to all users.
